propositions.text: The claimant is a Haitian citizen claiming refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: The refugee protection claimant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Haiti and is claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The claimant is a Haitian citizen claiming refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1), court states.

propositions.text: The panel considered Chairperson's Guideline 9 on sexual orientation and gender identity proceedings.
propositions.quote: In ruling on this refugee protection claim, the panel took into account the Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression.

paragraphs.summary: The panel considered Chairperson's Guideline 9 on sexual orientation and gender identity proceedings, court states.

propositions.text: The claimant states a priest promised him a US visa and money for sexual relations, leading to a homosexual relationship.
propositions.quote: He states that on his birthday on XXXX XXXX, 1984, an XXXX priest named XXXX XXXX summoned him into the rectory and promised him a US visa and money in exchange for sexual relations with him. The claimant accepted. After that first meeting, the claimant continued to go to the rectory and developed a homosexual relationship with the priest.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant states a priest promised him a US visa and money for sexual relations, leading to a homosexual relationship, claimant says.

propositions.text: The claimant was bullied and beaten for being called 'masi' and left his village for Port-au-Prince in 1985.
propositions.quote: The claimant states that he was bullied by his peers and that they beat him when he went to the rectory and called him "masi." On XXXX XXXX, 1985, the claimant left his village for Port-au-Prince, where he continued to practise homosexuality.

propositions.text: In Port-au-Prince, he was called 'masi' and assaulted in 1987, felt in danger, lived with a woman, and left for the Bahamas in 1998.
propositions.quote: In his neighbourhood, people called him "masi." On XXXX XXXX, 1987, he was physically assaulted by three strangers, who called him "masi." The claimant felt increasingly in danger, which is why he was living common-law with a woman. He left Haiti for the Bahamas on XXXX XXXX, 1998.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant was bullied and assaulted for being called 'masi', felt in danger, lived with a woman, and left Haiti for the Bahamas in 1998, claimant says.

propositions.text: In the Bahamas, claimant married a woman unaware of his orientation, practiced homosexuality secretly, faced bullying and assault in 2017.
propositions.quote: In 2006, in the Bahamas, he married XXXX XXXX XXXX, who was not aware of his sexual orientation. He states that he continued to practise homosexuality in secrecy. However, in the streets and at work, he was bullied and verbally assaulted because of his sexual orientation. On XXXX XXXX, 2017, he was assaulted.

propositions.text: He reported the 2017 assault to police who were hostile; he left Bahamas, went to US, then Canada in 2017 and claimed protection.
propositions.quote: He reported this incident to the police, who wrote him a report and told him, "I am not interesting in your gay business I wish the kill you and you better stop your stupidity." He decided to leave the Bahamas and arrived in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2017. He arrived in Canada on October 12, 2017, and filed a claim for protection at Fort Erie.

paragraphs.summary: In the Bahamas, claimant married a woman unaware of his orientation, faced bullying and assault, reported hostile police, left for US then Canada and claimed protection, claimant says.

propositions.text: The panel concludes claimant is a person referred to in Article 1E of the UN Refugee Convention.
propositions.quote: After considering the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant is a person referred to in Article 1E of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (the Convention).

paragraphs.summary: The panel concludes claimant is a person referred to in Article 1E of the UN Refugee Convention, court finds.

propositions.text: The panel finds claimant is not a Convention refugee under IRPA section 96 or person in need of protection under subsection 97(1).
propositions.quote: Moreover, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, for the reasons that follow.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under IRPA, court finds.

propositions.text: On Oct 18, 2018, IRB received Minister's opinion on possible exclusion under Article 1E due to claimant's permanent residence in Bahamas.
propositions.quote: On October 18, 2018, the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) received a Minister's opinion regarding a possible exclusion based on Article 1E of the Convention, given that it appears from the claimant's file that he was granted permanent residence in the Bahamas, as indicated by the stamp on page 27 of his Haitian passport and his permanent residence certificate issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012.

paragraphs.summary: On Oct 18, 2018, IRB received Minister's opinion on possible exclusion under Article 1E due to claimant's permanent residence in Bahamas, court states.

propositions.text: Section 98 IRPA excludes persons referred to in Article 1E or 1F of Refugee Convention from refugee or protection status.
propositions.quote: According to section 98 of the IRPA, "[a] person referred to in section E or F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection."

paragraphs.summary: Section 98 IRPA excludes persons referred to in Article 1E or 1F of Refugee Convention from refugee or protection status, statute states.

propositions.text: Article 1E excludes persons recognized by competent authorities as having rights like nationals of that country.
propositions.quote: Section E of Article 1 of the Convention is included in a schedule to the IRPA and reads as follows: E. This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country.

paragraphs.summary: Article 1E excludes persons recognized by competent authorities as having rights like nationals of that country, statute states.

propositions.text: Minister submits Article 1E applies because claimant has status in Bahamas conferring rights similar to nationals.
propositions.quote: In her notice of intervention, sent to the IRB and to the claimant, the Minister's representative submits that the information on the record demonstrates that: a. Section E of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention applies to the claimant because the evidence on the record shows that he has a status in the Bahamas that confers on him rights that are substantially similar to those of Bahamian nationals.

paragraphs.summary: Minister submits Article 1E applies because claimant has status in Bahamas conferring rights similar to nationals, Minister argues.

propositions.text: Minister argues claimant's permanent resident status in Bahamas excludes him from Convention protection.
propositions.quote: The Minister's representative submits that the evidence establishes a prima facie case that the claimant has permanent resident status in the Bahamas and is therefore excluded from the application of the Convention.

propositions.text: Minister argues abandoning permanent resident status shows no fear of returning to Haiti.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Minister's representative considers that voluntarily abandoning his permanent resident status in the Bahamas is not the behaviour of someone who allegedly fears returning to Haiti.

propositions.text: Minister states asylum shopping is incompatible with international refugee protection.
propositions.quote: She further states that asylum shopping is incompatible with the surrogate dimension of international refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: Minister argues claimant's permanent resident status excludes him, abandoning it shows no fear, and asylum shopping is incompatible with refugee protection, Minister argues.

propositions.text: Minister argues claimant's many trips to Haiti raise questions about fear, credibility, and claim merits.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Minister's representative is of the opinion that the significant number of trips to Haiti (Haitian entry and exit stamps in the claimant's passport) that the claimant has made since he left the country in XXXX 1998 raise legitimate questions about his subjective fear, his credibility and the merits of his claim for refugee protection.

propositions.text: Minister submits claimant stated to border officer he does not fear returning to Haiti or Bahamas, so claim should be rejected.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Minister's representative submits that the claimant himself stated in his sworn statement to a border services officer at the port of entry that he does not fear returning to Haiti or to the Bahamas. For these reasons, she is asking the panel to reject his refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: Minister argues claimant's trips to Haiti and statement of no fear undermine claim, so it should be rejected, Minister argues.

propositions.text: Panel questioned claimant about Bahamas status; claimant first said work permit, then confirmed permanent resident status and validity.
propositions.quote: During the hearing, the panel asked the claimant what his status in the Bahamas was, and he stated that he was a resident. The panel asked him what kind of residence permit he had, and he responded that he had a work permit. The panel then reminded him that his residence certificate states that he is a permanent resident of the Bahamas. He confirmed that he was a permanent resident of the Bahamas. The panel asked him whether, at the time of the hearing, his status was still valid, and the claimant answered that it was.

propositions.text: Claimant did not directly answer about residence permit type, so panel draws negative inference on credibility.
propositions.quote: First, the panel would like to point out that the claimant did not give a direct answer to the question about the kind of residence permit that he had in that country, and the panel therefore draws a negative inference regarding his credibility.

propositions.text: On hearing day, claimant was still a permanent resident of the Bahamas.
propositions.quote: Second, the panel notes that on the day of his hearing, the claimant was still a permanent resident of the Bahamas.

paragraphs.summary: Panel questioned claimant on Bahamas status; claimant first said work permit, then confirmed permanent resident; panel doubts credibility and notes status valid, court finds.

propositions.text: Panel concludes claimant has permanent resident status in Bahamas with rights similar to nationals, including health, education, employment.
propositions.quote: In light of the claimant's testimony, the panel concludes prima facie that the claimant has permanent resident status in the Bahamas, which gives him rights and obligations that are substantially similar to those of Bahamian nationals, including health care, education and employment rights.

paragraphs.summary: Panel concludes claimant has permanent resident status in Bahamas with rights similar to nationals, court finds.

propositions.text: Panel concludes claimant is a person referred to in Article 1E of the Convention.
propositions.quote: In light of the foregoing and having analyzed the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant is a person referred to in Article 1E of the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: Panel concludes claimant is a person referred to in Article 1E of the Convention, court finds.

propositions.text: Panel must determine if claimant can be excluded under Article 1E as permanent resident of Bahamas.
propositions.quote: First, the panel must determine whether the claimant can be excluded under Article 1E of the Convention because he is a permanent resident of the Bahamas.

paragraphs.summary: Panel must determine if claimant can be excluded under Article 1E as permanent resident of Bahamas, court states issue.

propositions.text: If claimant cannot return to Bahamas, panel will examine claim based on Haiti nationality.
propositions.quote: Second, if the claimant cannot return to the Bahamas, the panel will examine his claim based on his country of nationality, Haiti.

paragraphs.summary: If claimant cannot return to Bahamas, panel will examine claim based on Haiti nationality, court states issue.

propositions.text: Panel is satisfied claimant's identity as Haitian citizen established by testimony and passport copy.
propositions.quote: The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity as a citizen of Haiti, which was established by means of his testimony, as well as a copy of his passport issued by the Haitian authorities.

paragraphs.summary: Panel is satisfied claimant's identity as Haitian citizen established by testimony and passport copy, court finds.

propositions.text: Claimant submitted evidence establishing permanent resident status in Bahamas; panel concludes claimant established this.
propositions.quote: The claimant also submitted evidence to establish his permanent resident status in the Bahamas. After examining these documents, the panel concludes that the claimant has established that he is a permanent resident of the Bahamas.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant submitted evidence establishing permanent resident status in Bahamas; panel concludes claimant established this, court finds.

propositions.text: Claimants swearing facts true creates presumption of truth unless valid reasons to doubt exist.
propositions.quote: When claimants swear that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true,8 unless there are valid reasons to doubt their truthfulness.

propositions.text: Credibility finding is made on a balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The finding of whether or not a claimant's evidence is credible is made on a balance of probabilities.

paragraphs.summary: The court states claimants' sworn facts are presumed true unless doubted, and credibility is assessed on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: There were significant omissions and inconsistencies in the claimant's testimony about his alleged fears in the Bahamas.
propositions.quote: There were significant omissions and inconsistencies in the claimant's testimony about his alleged fears in the Bahamas.

propositions.text: The claimant's behaviour is inconsistent with that of a person fearing persecution in the Bahamas due to sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: Moreover, his behaviour is inconsistent with that of a person who allegedly fears persecution in the Bahamas by reason of his sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds significant omissions and inconsistencies in the claimant's testimony and behaviour inconsistent with fearing persecution in the Bahamas.

propositions.text: Claimant first had sexual relations with a man, the village priest, from 1984 to 1985 in his village.
propositions.quote: the claimant stated that he first had sexual relations with a man on XXXX XXXX, 1984, with the XXXX priest in his village, XXXX. He also stated that the relationship with the village priest lasted from XXXX to XXXX 1985.

propositions.text: People started suspecting the claimant and priest in late 1984 or early 1985, causing problems for claimant.
propositions.quote: people started to suspect that he and the priest were having sexual relations in late XXXX or early XXXX 1985 and that the suspicions caused problems for him.

propositions.text: Claimant left village for school but returned during vacations despite suspicions starting in late 1984 or early 1985.
propositions.quote: he went to Port-au-Prince for school and came back to the village during vacation periods... he continued to go back and forth between his village and Port-au-Prince until XXXX 1985.

propositions.text: Claimant said he left village for good in 1985 after a 'big fight' but did not mention this in his written account.
propositions.quote: he had left his village for good on XXXX XXXX, 1985, following a [translation] "big fight."... claimant did not specify that he left his village on XXXX XXXX, 1985, following a "big fight."

propositions.text: Panel draws negative inference on claimant's credibility and subjective fear due to omissions and unexplained returns to village.
propositions.quote: the panel draws a negative inference concerning the claimant's credibility and the problems he allegedly had in his village... further negative inference regarding the claimant's subjective fear because he did not provide a reasonable explanation for returning to his village

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant's testimony about his village relationship inconsistent and draws negative credibility and fear inferences.

propositions.text: Claimant had a romantic relationship with Mr. XXXX in the Bahamas from 2008 lasting eight years, living together in Nassau.
propositions.quote: he had had a romantic relationship with Mr. XXXX and lived with him for eight years in the Bahamas

propositions.text: Claimant did not mention Mr. XXXX in his written account despite relationship and living together.
propositions.quote: he was homosexual in the Bahamas, but had not mentioned Mr. XXXX... he had not put it down on paper

propositions.text: Panel finds it hard to believe claimant forgot to mention an eight-year romantic relationship and draws negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: The panel finds it hard to believe that the claimant would have had a romantic relationship with Mr. XXXX and lived with him for eight years in the Bahamas, yet forgotten to mention their romantic relationship in his account.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant's omission of an eight-year relationship in the Bahamas undermines his credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant alleged assault in Bahamas in 2017 by individuals calling him homosexual, filed police complaint same day.
propositions.quote: he was assaulted on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, in the Bahamas by a group of individuals who called him a homosexual... he filed a complaint with the police and a report was provided at the hearing.

propositions.text: Police report states assault occurred 'last month' not on the exact date claimant alleged.
propositions.quote: the report was prepared on XXXX XXXX, 2017. It states that "[the claimant] was approached last month by strangers who assaulted him because of his sexual orientation."

propositions.text: Panel finds claimant's explanation for police report inconsistency unsatisfactory and draws negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: this answer is not satisfactory... the panel draws a negative inference concerning the claimant's credibility with respect to the alleged attack

propositions.text: Panel gives no weight to police report to corroborate assault claim due to inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: the panel gives no weight to the police report to corroborate the attack on XXXX XXXX, 2017, allegedly because of the claimant's sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds inconsistencies in assault date and police report, drawing negative credibility inferences and giving no weight to the report.

propositions.text: Claimant stated marriage date and wife's birthdate but gave inconsistent answers about marriage date and his age at marriage.
propositions.quote: he got married on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2006... wife born on XXXX XXXX, 1954... claimant stated he was 42, then 40, then 42 at marriage, but was actually 47 in 2006.

propositions.text: Panel finds claimant adjusted answers due to contradictions and draws negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimant adjusted his answers based on the contradictions and therefore draws a negative inference regarding his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant's inconsistent marriage and age answers undermine his credibility.

propositions.text: Three versions of marriage certificate presented differ in certificate number and official who performed marriage.
propositions.quote: three different versions of the marriage certificate... certificate number in upper-right corner differs... person who performed the marriage differs

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker notes inconsistencies among three versions of the claimant's marriage certificate.

propositions.text: Claimant brought photocopies of marriage certificate, left original with wife, and could not explain inconsistencies in certificate numbers.
propositions.quote: claimant stated that he had not brought the original with him from the Bahamas... these were photocopies... he did not know what had happened

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant unable to explain inconsistencies in photocopies of marriage certificate.

propositions.text: Claimant could not explain inconsistencies about who performed the marriage on certificates.
propositions.quote: claimant stated that he did not know, that it was his marriage certificate

propositions.text: Panel not satisfied claimant provided acceptable marriage documents and draws negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: panel is not satisfied that the claimant has provided acceptable documents establishing that he was married... draws a negative inference concerning the claimant's overall credibility

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant's marriage documents unacceptable and draws negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: Claimant said he and wife separated in 2008 after she found out he was homosexual.
propositions.quote: he and his wife had separated... when Ms. XXXX had found out that he was homosexual... separated in 2008

propositions.text: Claimant told CBSA officer in 2017 separation was 2-3 years ago, inconsistent with 2008 separation claim.
propositions.quote: he answered, "2 - 3 years, but she talks with me all the time."... panel pointed out difference between 10 years and 2-3 years

propositions.text: Panel not satisfied with claimant's explanation for inconsistency, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: panel is not satisfied with the claimant's answers... his explanation is not reasonable. The claimant's credibility is again undermined.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant's inconsistent separation dates undermine his credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant provided letter from ex-wife stating she found out he was homosexual and wants marriage dissolved.
propositions.quote: Ms. XXXX states that she "found out that her husband [XXXX XXXX] is homosexual" and... "wants the marriage dissolved."

propositions.text: Panel gives no weight to ex-wife's letter due to concerns about marriage certificate and separation date inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: panel gives no weight to this letter as corroboration of the claimant's sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker gives no weight to ex-wife's letter due to other credibility concerns.

propositions.text: Panel finds letter from Executive Director of XXXX XXXX organization has no probative value due to credibility issues.
propositions.quote: panel finds that this document has no probative value.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds the letter from the organization has no probative value due to credibility issues.

propositions.text: Claimant made multiple round trips to Haiti via US after 2008 but never claimed protection in US.
propositions.quote: claimant had made a number of round trips to Haiti, always with a stopover in the United States... he never claimed protection in the United States.

propositions.text: Claimant said he did not claim protection in US because he did not know anyone and only decided to claim in Canada after sister's advice.
propositions.quote: he did not claim protection in the United States because he did not know anyone there... when his sister told him that it was possible to claim protection in Canada that he decided to come here.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker notes claimant's multiple US stopovers without asylum claims and his explanation for not claiming protection there.

propositions.text: Federal Court confirmed it is reasonable to conclude that returning to feared country makes subjective fear unlikely.
propositions.quote: Federal Court has confirmed that it is reasonable to conclude that a claimant returning to the country where he or she feared persecution makes the existence of such a fear unlikely.

propositions.text: In Kabengele, Refugee Division may consider claimant's actions returning to feared country in assessing subjective fear.
propositions.quote: It is quite proper for the Refugee Division to take the plaintiff's actions into account in assessing his subjective fear.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court in Kabengele confirms returning to feared country undermines subjective fear assessment.

propositions.text: Claimant's failure to claim asylum in US during multiple stopovers undermines credibility of subjective fear of returning to Bahamas.
propositions.quote: claimant's failure to claim asylum in the United States during his multiple stopovers there... undermines the credibility of his subjective fear of returning to the Bahamas

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds claimant's failure to claim asylum in US undermines his subjective fear credibility.

propositions.text: Panel does not believe there is enough evidence to establish claimant's reasonable fear of persecution in Bahamas due to sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: the panel does not believe that there is enough evidence in this case to establish that the claimant would have a reasonable fear of persecution by reason of his sexual orientation if he were to return to the Bahamas.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker concludes insufficient evidence exists to establish claimant's reasonable fear of persecution in Bahamas.

propositions.text: Claimant is excluded under Article 1E of the UN Refugee Convention due to permanent resident status in Bahamas.
propositions.quote: the panel concludes that the claimant, XXXX XXXX, is excluded under Article 1E of the United Nations Refugee Convention, because he has permanent resident status in the Bahamas

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant is excluded under Article 1E of the UN Refugee Convention due to Bahamas permanent resident status.

propositions.text: Pursuant to section 98 of IRPA, claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: pursuant to section 98 of the IRPA, since the claimant is a person referred to in section E of Article 1 of the Convention, he is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection."

paragraphs.summary: The court orders claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under IRPA section 98.

propositions.text: Panel determines claimant is excluded under the Convention.
propositions.quote: the panel determines that XXXX XXXX is excluded under the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The court determines claimant is excluded under the Convention.
